edition: Newton, Principia, Andrew Motte trans., 1729 (Wikisource); Book I, Section I, Lemma II; Plate 1, Fig. 6.

figures.caption: If in any figure AacE there be inscribed parallelograms on equal bases and circumscribed parallelograms completed: as the bases are diminished without limit, the inscribed, circumscribed, and curvilinear figures have the ultimate ratio of equality.

text.latex:
Newton considers a plane figure $AacE$ bounded by the straight side \textcolor{base}{Aa},
the baseline \textcolor{base}{AE}, and the curve \textcolor{curve}{acE}.
The baseline is divided into the equal bases $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, so that \textcolor{base}{the base}
is partitioned into segments of one common breadth.
The whole question concerns the area enclosed beneath \textcolor{curve}{the curve} —
for it is \textcolor{curve}{this curve} that is the heart of the figure and of the Lemma.

Within the figure Newton inscribes \textcolor{insc}{the parallelograms $Ab$, $Bc$, $Cd$},
each raised on one of the equal bases and reaching upward only to the lower vertex
of \textcolor{curve}{the curve} on that base.
Because \textcolor{insc}{each inscribed rectangle} stops short of \textcolor{curve}{the curve},
their united area — the step-figure $AKbLcMdD$ — lies \textcolor{insc}{entirely below} it.
Thus \textcolor{insc}{the inscribed figure} is a deficient approximation, always less than
the true curvilinear area.

Finally Newton circumscribes \textcolor{circ}{the parallelograms $aKbl$, $bLcm$, $cMdn$},
each rising above \textcolor{curve}{the curve} to its upper vertex.
The difference between \textcolor{circ}{the circumscribed figure} and the inscribed figure
is the sum of the little tops $Kl$, $Lm$, $Mn$, $Do$; since all bases are equal,
this sum is \textcolor{excess}{the single rectangle $ABla$}, of breadth $AB$ and height $Aa$.
But as $AB$ is diminished $in\ infinitum$, \textcolor{excess}{this rectangle} becomes less
than any given space, so by Lemma~I the inscribed and \textcolor{circ}{circumscribed} figures
become ultimately equal, and $much\ more$ is \textcolor{curve}{the intermediate curvilinear figure}
equal to either.
$Q.E.D.$
